column1: # Jāmiʿ al-ʿUlūm wa-l-Ḥikam — Hadith 49: “If you relied on Allah as He truly deserves to be relied upon”

column2: From ʿUmar ibn al-Khaṭṭāb (may Allah be pleased with him), from the Prophet ﷺ, who said: “If you relied on Allah as He truly deserves to be relied upon, He would provide for you as He provides for the birds:

they go out hungry in the morning and come back full in the evening.” Imam Aḥmad, al-Tirmidhī, al-Nasāʾī, Ibn Mājah, Ibn Ḥibbān in his Ṣaḥīḥ, and al-Ḥākim reported it, and al-Tirmidhī said: Good and authentic (ḥasan ṣaḥīḥ).
All of these recorded this hadith through the narration of ʿAbdullāh ibn Hubayrah, who heard Abū Tamīm al-Jayshānī, who heard ʿUmar ibn al-Khaṭṭāb narrating it from the Prophet ﷺ.

Muslim recorded narrations of both Abū Tamīm and ʿAbdullāh ibn Hubayrah, and more than one critic declared them reliable. Abū Tamīm was born in the lifetime of the Prophet ﷺ and emigrated to Madīnah in the time of ʿUmar (may Allah be pleased with him).
This hadith has also been narrated from the hadith of Ibn ʿUmar, from the Prophet ﷺ, but its chain contains someone whose condition is unknown.
Abū Ḥātim al-Rāzī said this.

This hadith is a foundation for reliance on Allah (tawakkul), and shows that it is among the greatest means by which provision is drawn. Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, said: “Whoever fears Allah, He will make a way out for him and provide for him from where he does not expect; and whoever relies on Allah, He is sufficient for him” [al-Ṭalāq 65:2–3].
The Prophet ﷺ recited this verse to Abū Dharr and said to him: “If all people took hold of it, it would suffice them” — meaning that if they truly realised taqwā and reliance,
that would suffice them for the interests of their religion and their worldly life.
This meaning was discussed earlier, in the commentary on the hadith of Ibn ʿAbbās: “Be mindful of Allah, and He will protect you.”
One of the Salaf said: It is enough for you, as a means of approaching Him, that He knows from your heart how well you rely on Him. How many of His servants have entrusted their affairs to Him,
and He has spared them what worried them! Then he recited: “Whoever fears Allah, He will make a way out for him and provide for him from where he does not expect” [al-Ṭalāq 65:2–3].

The reality of reliance is the heart's true dependence on Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, for bringing about benefits and warding off harms in all the affairs of this world and the Hereafter; the entrusting of all affairs to Him; and the true conviction that none but He gives or withholds, harms or benefits.
Saʿīd ibn Jubayr said: Reliance is the sum of faith.
Wahb ibn Munabbih said: The furthest goal is reliance.
Al-Ḥasan said: The servant's reliance on his Lord is that he knows that Allah is the One in whom he trusts.
In the hadith of Ibn ʿAbbās, the Prophet ﷺ said: “Whoever would like to be the strongest of people, let him rely on Allah.”

It is narrated of him ﷺ that he used to say in his supplication, “O Allah, I ask You for true reliance on You,” and that he used to say, “O Allah, make me one of those who relied on You and whom You sufficed.”

Know that truly realising reliance does not conflict with striving through the means by which Allah, Glorified is He, has decreed what He decrees, and which His way (sunnah) with His creation has followed. Allah the Exalted commanded the taking of means along with His command to rely on Him; so striving through the means with one's limbs is obedience to Him,

and relying on Him with one's heart is faith in Him. As Allah the Exalted said: “O you who believe, take your precautions” [al-Nisāʾ 4:71]; and He said: “Prepare against them whatever force you can, and tethered horses” [al-Anfāl 8:60]; and He said: “When the prayer is finished, disperse through the land and seek of Allah's bounty” [al-Jumuʿah 62:10].
Sahl al-Tustarī said: Whoever disparages movement — meaning striving and earning — has disparaged the Sunnah, and whoever disparages reliance
has disparaged faith. Reliance is the state of the Prophet ﷺ, and earning is his Sunnah; so whoever acts according to his state, let him not abandon his Sunnah.
The deeds a servant does, moreover, are of three kinds.

The first is the acts of obedience that Allah has commanded His servants to do and made a means of salvation from the Fire and of entering Paradise. These must be done, while relying on Allah in doing them and seeking His help for them,

for there is no might and no power except through Him: what He wills is, and what He does not will is not. Whoever falls short in any of what is obligatory on him here deserves punishment in this world and the Hereafter, both by the Sharīʿah and by decree.
Yūsuf ibn Asbāṭ said: It used to be said: Work as a man who will be saved only by his work, and rely as a man who will be struck only by what has been written for him.

The second is what Allah has made the customary course in this world and commanded His servants to engage in, such as eating when hungry, drinking when thirsty, seeking shade from the heat and warming oneself against the cold. Here too a person must take the means,

and whoever falls short in this, so that he is harmed by leaving it when he was able to use it, is negligent and deserves punishment. Allah, Glorified is He, may, however, strengthen some of His servants in this for what others cannot endure;

and if such a person acts according to the strength by which he is singled out from others, there is no blame on him. That is why the Prophet ﷺ used to fast continuously without breaking his fast, while forbidding his Companions to do so,

telling them: “I am not like you; I am given food and drink.” In one narration: “I spend the day with my Lord, and He feeds me and gives me drink”; and in another: “I have one who feeds me and one who gives me drink.”

What seems most likely is that he meant that Allah strengthens and nourishes him with what He brings to his heart of holy openings, divine gifts and lordly knowledge, which free him of the need for food and drink for a stretch of time, as the poet said:
She has tales of remembering you that keep her / from drink, and distract her from provision.
She has a light from your face by which she sees her way / as she travels, and behind her a driver sings.
When she complains of the weariness of the road, the joy / of arrival makes her a promise, and at the promised time she revives.
So she does not hunger or thirst, nor does she weaken, / nor does she lose her way, since she has a guide.
Many of the Salaf had a capacity for going without food and drink that others did not have, and they were not harmed by it.
Ibn al-Zubayr used to fast continuously for eight days.
Abū al-Jawzāʾ used to join his fasts across seven days, and then grip a young man's forearm and almost crush it.
Ibrāhīm al-Taymī would stay two months eating nothing, though he would drink a sweet drink.
Ḥajjāj ibn Furāfiṣah would go more than ten days without eating, drinking or sleeping.

Some of them paid no heed to heat or cold. ʿAlī (may Allah be pleased with him), for instance, used to wear summer clothes in winter and winter clothes in summer, for the Prophet ﷺ had prayed for him that Allah would take heat and cold away from him.

Whoever has the strength for things like these and acts according to his strength, without its weakening him from obeying Allah, is not to blame. But whoever burdens himself with it until it weakens him from some of his obligations
is to be rebuked for it. The Salaf used to rebuke ʿAbd al-Raḥmān ibn Abī Nuʿm because he would go without eating for so long that people had to visit him [as an invalid] because of his weakness.

The third kind is what Allah has made the customary course in this world in the great majority of cases, though He may break the custom in it for whichever of His servants He wills. It is of several types.
One of them is what He often breaks, freeing many of His creatures from the need for it, such as medicines, in many lands and for desert-dwellers and the like.
The scholars have disagreed over which is better for someone who falls ill: to seek treatment, or — for one who has truly realised reliance on Allah — to leave it.

There are two well-known views on this. The apparent sense of Aḥmad's words is that reliance is better for one who has the strength for it, because of what is authentically reported from the Prophet ﷺ, that he said:

“Seventy thousand of my nation will enter Paradise without reckoning.” Then he said: “They are those who do not take evil omens, do not ask others to recite incantations over them, do not have themselves cauterised, and rely on their Lord.”

Those who preferred treatment said: It was the state of the Prophet ﷺ, which he kept to constantly, and he does only what is best. They understood the hadith to refer to disliked incantations from which shirk is feared, the proof being that he joined them with cauterisation and taking omens, both of which are disliked.

Another is what He breaks for a few of the common people, such as provision coming to someone who has given up striving to seek it. Whoever Allah has granted true certainty and reliance, and knows from Allah that He breaks customs for him
and does not make him need the usual means of seeking provision and the like, may give up the means, and he is not to be rebuked for it. This hadith of ʿUmar that we are discussing indicates as much,

and indicates that people are let down only by their failure to realise reliance truly, and by their hearts' stopping at the outward means and resting on them. That is why they wear themselves out in the means and strive in them to the utmost, and nothing comes to them except what has been decreed for them.

If they truly realised reliance on Allah in their hearts, Allah would drive their provision to them with the slightest of means, as He drives to the birds their provision merely by their going out in the morning and returning in the evening. That is a kind of seeking and striving, but a light one.

A person may also be deprived of his provision, or part of it, because of a sin he commits, as in the hadith of Thawbān, from the Prophet ﷺ: “A servant is deprived of provision because of a sin he commits.”

In the hadith of Jābir, from the Prophet ﷺ: “No soul will die until it has received its provision in full; so fear Allah and be moderate in seeking it: take what is lawful and leave what is unlawful.”

ʿUmar said: Between the servant and his provision there is a veil. If he is content and his soul is satisfied, his provision comes to him; and if he rushes in and tears the veil, he gets no more than his provision.
One of the Salaf said: Rely [on Allah], and provision will be driven to you without toil or strain.

Sālim ibn Abī al-Jaʿd said: I was told that ʿĪsā (peace be upon him) used to say: Work for Allah and do not work for your stomachs. Beware of the excesses of this world, for the excesses of this world are filth in the sight of Allah. Here are the birds of the sky: they go out in the morning and return in the evening carrying none of their provision with them;

they neither plough nor reap, and Allah provides for them. If you say, “Our stomachs are bigger than the stomachs of birds,” then here are the wild beasts — wild cattle, wild asses and others: they go out in the morning and return in the evening carrying none of their provision with them; they neither plough nor reap, and Allah provides for them.
Ibn Abī al-Dunyā recorded it.

He recorded with his chain from Ibn ʿAbbās, who said: A worshipper used to worship in a cave, and a raven would bring him a loaf every day in which he found the taste of everything, until that worshipper died.

From Saʿīd ibn ʿAbd al-ʿAzīz, from some of the elders of Damascus, who said: Ilyās stayed on a mountain, fleeing from his people, for twenty nights — or he said, forty — and the ravens brought him his provision.

Sufyān al-Thawrī said: Wāṣil al-Aḥdab recited this verse, “And in the heaven is your provision and what you are promised” [al-Dhāriyāt 51:22], and said: Is my provision in the heaven, while I seek it on the earth?

So he went into a ruin and stayed there three days without getting anything. On the fourth day, there was a basket of fresh dates. He had a brother whose intention was better than his, who went in with him, and it became two baskets. That remained their way until death parted them.

Of this kind too is the one whose reliance on Allah and trust in Him are strong, so that he enters the desert without provisions. This is permissible for one so described, but not for one who has not reached this station.

He has a model in this in Ibrāhīm, the Friend of Allah (peace be upon him), who left Hājar and her son Ismāʿīl in a valley without crops, leaving with them a leather bag of dates and a waterskin of water. When Hājar followed him and said to him:
To whom are you leaving us?

He said to her: To Allah. She said: I am content with Allah. He did this by Allah's command and revelation. Allah may cast into the hearts of some of His friends true inspiration that they know to be true and in which they trust.
Al-Marrūdhī said: Abū ʿAbdillāh was asked: What is true reliance on Allah?
He said: That one relies on Allah and has no human being in his heart from whom he hopes that something will come to him. If he is like that, Allah will provide for him, and he is one who relies.
He said: I mentioned reliance to Abū ʿAbdillāh, and he allowed it for one who practises it truthfully.
He said: I asked Abū ʿAbdillāh about a man who sits at home, saying, “I will sit and be patient and not let anyone know of it,” though he is able to work at a trade.
He said: If he went out and worked at a trade, I would prefer it. If he sits, I fear it will lead him to expecting that something be sent to him.
I said: And if something is sent to him, he does not take it?
He said: That is good.

I said to Abū ʿAbdillāh: A man in Makkah said, “I will eat nothing until they feed me,” and went into the mountain of Abū Qubays. Two men came to him while he had nothing on but a rag round his waist, and threw him a shirt;

they took him by the hands and put the shirt on him, and set something before him, but he would not eat until they put an iron key in his mouth and began pushing food into it. Abū ʿAbdillāh laughed and was filled with wonder.

I said to Abū ʿAbdillāh: A man gave up buying and selling, made it binding on himself that no gold or silver would come into his hand, and left his houses without giving any instructions about them. He would walk along the road, and if he saw something lying there that had been thrown away, he would take it.

Al-Marrūdhī said: I said to the man: You have no precedent for this except Abū Muʿāwiyah al-Aswad. He said: No — Uways al-Qaranī; he used to pass by the rubbish heaps and pick up scraps of cloth. He said: Abū ʿAbdillāh confirmed what he said, and said: He has been hard on himself.
Then he said: Al-Baqlī and others like him came to me, and I said to them: Why not take up work? You are making yourselves conspicuous. He said: What do we care about being conspicuous?

Aḥmad ibn al-Ḥusayn ibn Ḥassān narrated from Aḥmad that he was asked about a man who sets out for Makkah without provisions. He said: If you can bear it, [go]; otherwise not, except with provisions and a mount. Do not take risks.

Abū Bakr al-Khallāl said: That is, if he can bear it and knows that he is strong enough for it, does not beg, and his soul does not look expectantly to taking, or to being given and accepting, then he is relying in truth; and the scholars have permitted reliance in truth.
He said: Abū ʿAbdillāh made the Ḥajj, and fourteen dirhams were enough for him on his pilgrimage.
Isḥāq ibn Rāhawayh was asked: May a man enter the desert without provisions?

He said: If the man is like ʿAbdullāh ibn Munīr, he may enter the desert without provisions; otherwise he may not. When a man is weak, and fears for himself that he will not be patient, or that he will expose himself to begging,

or fall into doubt and discontent, it is not permissible for him to give up the means in that case, and he is to be rebuked in the strongest terms, as Imam Aḥmad and others rebuked one who gave up earning and one who entered the desert without provisions, fearing that he would expose himself to begging.
It has been narrated that Ibn ʿAbbās said: The people of Yemen used to go on Ḥajj without taking provisions, saying:

We are those who rely [on Allah]. They would make the Ḥajj, come to Makkah and beg from people; so Allah revealed this verse: “And take provisions, but the best provision is taqwā” [al-Baqarah 2:197]. Mujāhid, ʿIkrimah,
al-Nakhaʿī and more than one of the Salaf said the same. So no concession is given for abandoning means altogether except to one whose heart has entirely ceased to look expectantly to created beings.

It is narrated that Aḥmad was asked about reliance and said: It is cutting off expectation by despairing of creatures. He was asked for the proof of this, and said: The words of Ibrāhīm (peace be upon him) when Jibrīl appeared to him as he was being thrown into the fire and said to him: Do you have any need?
He said: Of you — no.

The apparent sense of Aḥmad's words is that earning is better in every case. He was asked about someone who sits and does not earn, saying, “I rely on Allah,” and said: All people ought to rely on Allah, but they should provide for themselves by earning.

Al-Khallāl narrated with his chain from al-Fuḍayl ibn ʿIyāḍ that he was asked: What if a man sat at home, claiming that he trusts Allah to bring him his provision? He said: If he trusted Allah, so that He knew from him that he truly trusted Him, nothing he wanted would be withheld from him;
but neither the prophets nor anyone else did this. The prophets used to hire themselves out; the Prophet ﷺ hired himself out, as did Abū Bakr and ʿUmar,

and they did not say: We will sit until Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, provides for us. Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, has said: “And seek of Allah's bounty” [al-Jumuʿah 62:10]. One must seek a livelihood.

Something suggesting otherwise has been narrated from Bishr. Abū Nuʿaym narrated in al-Ḥilyah that Bishr was asked about reliance and said: Motion without stillness, and stillness without motion. The questioner said to him:

Explain it to us so that we may understand. Bishr said: Motion without stillness is a man whose limbs are in motion while his heart is still, resting on Allah and not on his work. Stillness without motion is a man resting on Allah without any movement; this is rare, and it is one of the qualities of the abdāl [the saintly substitutes].

In any case, whoever has not reached these lofty stations must attend to the means, especially if he has dependants who cannot be patient. The Prophet ﷺ said: “It is sin enough for a man that he neglects those he must provide for.”
Bishr used to say: If I had dependants, I would work and earn.

Likewise, whoever loses a right of his by abandoning the means, and is not content to see it lost, is helpless and negligent. It is of such a person that the Prophet ﷺ said: “The strong believer is better and dearer to Allah than the weak believer, and in both there is good.

Be eager for what benefits you, seek Allah's help and do not be helpless. If something befalls you, do not say, ‘If only I had done such-and-such, it would have been so-and-so’; rather say, ‘Allah has decreed, and He did what He willed,’ for ‘if only’ opens the door to the work of Satan.” Muslim recorded something with this meaning from the hadith of Abū Hurayrah.
In the Sunan of Abū Dāwūd, from ʿAwf ibn Mālik: The Prophet ﷺ gave judgement between two men, and the one judged against said as he turned away:

Allah is sufficient for us, and He is the best Disposer of affairs. The Prophet ﷺ said: “Allah blames helplessness. You should rather act shrewdly; then, if something overcomes you, say: Allah is sufficient for me, and He is the best Disposer of affairs.”
Al-Tirmidhī recorded from the hadith of Anas, who said: A man said: Messenger of Allah, shall I tie her up [my camel] and rely [on Allah], or leave her loose and rely?
He said: “Tie her up and rely.”
He mentioned that Yaḥyā al-Qaṭṭān said: In my view it is an objectionable (munkar) hadith.
Al-Ṭabarānī recorded it from the hadith of ʿAmr ibn Umayyah, from the Prophet ﷺ.
Al-Waḍīn ibn ʿAṭāʾ narrated from Maḥfūẓ ibn ʿAlqamah, from Ibn ʿĀʾidh, that the Prophet ﷺ said: “Reliance comes after shrewdness.” This is mursal.

It means that a person acts shrewdly, striving through permissible means, and relies on Allah after his striving. All of this points to the fact that reliance does not conflict with taking the means; indeed, combining the two may be better.
Muʿāwiyah ibn Qurrah said: ʿUmar ibn al-Khaṭṭāb met some people from Yemen and said: Who are you?

They said: We are those who rely (al-mutawakkilūn). He said: No, you are those who live off others (al-mutaʾakkilūn). The one who relies is the one who casts his seed into the ground and relies on Allah, the Mighty and Majestic.
Al-Khallāl said: Muḥammad ibn Aḥmad ibn Manṣūr informed us: Al-Māzinī asked Bishr ibn al-Ḥārith about reliance, and he said: The one who relies does not rely on Allah in order to be provided for.

If this notion settled in the hearts of those who rely, they would cry out to Allah in remorse and repentance. Rather, the one who relies settles in his heart that his sufficiency comes from Allah, Blessed and Exalted is He, and so he believes Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, in what He has guaranteed.
What these words mean is that one who relies on Allah as He truly deserves does not practise reliance and make it a means of obtaining sufficiency from Allah, in provision and other things;
for if he did so, he would be like one who takes any other means in order to draw provision and sufficiency through it, and this is a kind of deficiency in truly realising reliance.
The one who truly relies is rather the one who knows that Allah has guaranteed His servant his provision and sufficiency, so he believes Allah in what He has guaranteed, trusts Him with his heart,
and truly depends on Him for the provision He has guaranteed, without treating reliance as one of the means of drawing provision. Provision is apportioned to everyone, righteous and wicked,

believer and disbeliever, as the Exalted said: “There is no creature on the earth but its provision is upon Allah” [Hūd 11:6] — and this despite the weakness of many creatures and their inability to strive in seeking provision. The Exalted said: “How many a creature does not carry its own provision! Allah provides for it and for you” [al-ʿAnkabūt 29:60].

So long as the servant is alive, his provision is upon Allah, and Allah may make it easy for him with earning or without it. Whoever relies on Allah in order to seek provision has made reliance a means and a form of earning; and whoever relies on Him because he trusts His guarantee

has relied on Him out of trust and belief in Him. How excellent are the words of Muthannā al-Anbārī, one of the most eminent of Imam Aḥmad's companions: Do not be anxious about what is guaranteed, lest you suspect the Guarantor and be discontent with His provision.

Know that the fruit of reliance is contentment with the decree. Whoever entrusts his affairs to Allah and is content with what He decrees and chooses for him has truly realised reliance on Him. That is why al-Ḥasan, al-Fuḍayl and others explained reliance on Allah as contentment.

Ibn Abī al-Dunyā said: It has reached me that one of the sages said: Reliance has three degrees: the first is giving up complaint, the second is contentment and the third is love. Giving up complaint is the degree of patience;

contentment is the heart's being at rest with what Allah has apportioned for it, and it is higher than the first; and love is that one loves what Allah does with one. The first is for the ascetics, the second for the truthful, and the third for the messengers. End of quotation.

So if the one who relies on Allah is patient with what Allah decrees for him of provision or anything else, he is patient; if he is content with what is decreed for him after it has happened, he is content;

and if he has no choice of his own at all, and no contentment except in what is decreed for him, that is the degree of the lovers who know Allah (al-ʿārifūn) — as ʿUmar ibn ʿAbd al-ʿAzīz used to say: I have woken this morning with no joy except in the places where decree and destiny fall.
